The student was not talking about losing his academic classes. "Courses" here means the dishes of a meal. As part of a University of Hong Kong formal dinner event, he had a deadline to choose his meal courses in advance, and he chose them. At the dinner that evening, the courses were served one after another and he ate them all. By the end of the evening, every course he had chosen was gone—consumed—so "all of my courses were gone in one evening" refers to his meal courses being eaten, not to his university courses disappearing.

The student was talking about meal courses for a University of Hong Kong hall/formal dinner, not academic classes. He had a deadline to book his meal courses, and he chose them in advance. However, those booked courses were given to someone else or otherwise not eaten by him, and at the dinner they were cleared away uneaten even though he was present. So "all of my courses were gone in one evening" means his ordered dinner courses were taken/cleared away that evening—not that his university course selections had vanished. The trick is the double meaning of "courses": academic classes versus served dishes; here it is the dinner dishes that were gone.

The student was not talking about his academic classes. "Courses" here means the dishes of a meal at a University of Hong Kong hall/formal dinner. He had to choose his meal courses before a booking deadline, and he did so. On the evening of the dinner, however, those courses were not eaten by him: the food was cleared away uneaten even though he was present—taken from the table, with the staff clearing it. Thus "all of my courses were gone in one evening" refers to his ordered dinner courses disappearing/being cleared that evening, playing on the two meanings of "courses" (university classes versus dishes served at a meal). The apparent academic enrollment problem is a misunderstanding; the real event was about meal courses at a dinner.
